planting.note: Root short tip cuttings in moist sphagnum or a peat-based mix under high humidity, then press the trailing stems against damp terrarium substrate, wood, or backgrounds where the fine aerial roots will cling and spread on their own.

directions: This dwarf cultivar of creeping fig carries small, deeply lobed juvenile leaves shaped like miniature oak leaves, held tight against thin wiry stems that cling to bark, cork, and terrarium glass with fine adhesive aerial roots. Kept in its creeping juvenile form indefinitely under terrarium conditions, it never produces the thick leathery adult foliage or fruit seen when the species is allowed to climb into full sun outdoors, instead forming a dense, low, textured mat or curtain over hardscape. It prefers bright indirect light and evenly moist, well-drained substrate, and tolerates the humid, enclosed air of a closed terrarium or vivarium far better than typical houseplant conditions. Trim regularly to keep growth in check, since even the miniature form spreads vigorously once established and will climb any damp vertical surface offered to it.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Ficus pumila
North Carolina State University Extension — Ficus pumila

planting.note: Root short tip cuttings in moist sphagnum under high humidity, then lay the trailing stems over damp terrarium substrate, cork bark, or foam backgrounds; the tiny aerial roots grip on contact and the mat fills in from there.

directions: A finer-textured selection of creeping fig, this cultivar bears juvenile leaves scarcely a quarter to half inch long that overlap densely along thread-like stems, producing a close, moss-like carpet rather than the coarser mat of the straight species. It is one of the most popular living groundcovers for terrarium and vivarium floors and backgrounds because its small scale stays in proportion even in a nano enclosure, and it self-attaches to damp bark, foam, or stone without any need for pinning. Give it bright indirect light and steady moisture; it tolerates the saturated air of a closed terrarium well but will also grow in a humid open container with regular misting. Left untrimmed it climbs and cascades readily, so shear back runners periodically to keep the miniature form dense and low.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Ficus pumila
North Carolina State University Extension — Ficus pumila

planting.note: Root stem cuttings under high humidity or set out terrarium-grown starts in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full shade; give this cultivar the same closed, humid conditions as other fittonias since dry air causes rapid wilting.

directions: Pink Angel carries the same oval, quilted leaves as other nerve plant selections, but the fine venation is overlaid with a soft rose-pink blush that spreads across much of the leaf surface rather than staying confined to thin veins, giving the foliage a warmer, more saturated color than the white- or red-veined forms. It shares the compact, spreading habit typical of albivenis cultivars and works well tucked among mosses and small ferns in a terrarium or paludarium planting. Humidity is non-negotiable: leaves go limp within hours in dry room air and only fully recover once enclosed conditions or heavy misting are restored, so open-room culture is best avoided. Keep the substrate evenly moist and warm, and pinch growing tips occasionally to keep the mat dense rather than leggy.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Fittonia albivenis

common_name: Mini Red Fittonia (Dwarf Red-Veined Nerve Plant)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings under high humidity or plant terrarium-grown starts in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full shade; this dwarf selection is best suited to terrariums and dish gardens rather than open containers.

directions: Mini Red is a compact companion to the more widely grown Mini White, bearing small, closely set oval leaves netted in deep red-copper veining over a dark olive-green background, on the same tight, low-growing frame that keeps its footprint in scale with small terrarium and vivarium plantings. Like every nerve plant it wilts dramatically the moment humidity drops and springs back once conditions are restored, making it far better suited to closed terrariums, bottle gardens, and misted vivarium floors than open-air pots. Keep the substrate evenly moist and warm, provide bright but indirect light, and take tip cuttings regularly both to propagate new plants and to keep the low mat from thinning out.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Fittonia albivenis

planting.note: Divide established clumps or set small rooted sprigs directly into constantly moist, humus-rich terrarium substrate in full shade; this tropical spikemoss has no drought tolerance and needs enclosed, high-humidity conditions to thrive.

directions: Native to the humid forest floor of Mexico and Central America, this spikemoss forms soft, ferny-textured mounds of finely branched, scale-covered stems in a pale, yellow-tinged green that reads almost lime-colored against darker terrarium companions. Its lax, slightly upright-then-arching growth habit sets it apart from the flatter creeping mats of kraussiana types, giving terrarium plantings some textural height without any true stem woodiness. Like all tropical selaginellas it has no drought tolerance whatsoever and must be kept constantly moist in a closed terrarium or vivarium with still, humid air; it browns and crisps within a day or two of exposure to dry room conditions. Bright indirect light keeps the color from fading, while any direct sun scorches the delicate foliage almost immediately.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Selaginella species
Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History — Selaginellaceae

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in a fast-draining, humid propagation mix, then transplant into a chunky, well-drained terrarium or hanging-basket mix; let the surface dry slightly between waterings rather than keeping it saturated like most terrarium pileas.

directions: Cedar Pilea bears small, thick, rounded leaves with a soft silvery-blue-gray cast and a slightly puckered, succulent texture, carried on trailing stems that cascade attractively over the edge of a raised terrarium planter, hanging basket, or open vivarium ledge. Crushed foliage releases a resinous, cedar-like scent that distinguishes it from the more strictly moisture-loving pileas such as glauca and depressa. Because its leaves store some water, it tolerates the substrate drying slightly between waterings and is more forgiving of the drier microclimates near terrarium lids or vents than typical companion foliage. Bright, filtered light keeps the silvery coloring vivid and the habit compact; low light causes noticeably longer, sparser stems.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Pilea species
North Carolina State University Extension — Pilea

common_name: Ornamental Pepper Vine (Red-Vein Pepper, Celebes Pepper)

planting.note: Root single-node stem cuttings in moist sphagnum under high humidity, then train the climbing stems onto cork bark, wood, or a trellis in a tall terrarium or vivarium where constant moisture and still, humid air are easy to maintain.

directions: This climbing tropical pepper relative carries heart-shaped, quilted leaves in deep green overlaid with an iridescent silvery-pink pattern that traces the veins, with contrasting burgundy-red undersides and stems that add color even when the vine is not in view head-on. In cultivation it climbs by clinging roots along damp bark or trellis supports, making it a popular background and vertical accent plant in tall bioactive vivariums and paludariums. It demands the same constant warmth and saturated humidity as its rainforest floor origin and struggles badly in open, dry household air, so it is best reserved for enclosed terrarium or vivarium culture. Keep the substrate evenly moist, provide bright indirect light, and pinch growing tips to encourage bushier, fuller climbing growth rather than a single sparse runner.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Piper species
Kew Plants of the World Online — Piper crocatum
